gaps.sentence: I ___ rather stay at home tonight, if that is all right.
gaps.explanation: 'Would rather' expresses preference: would rather stay.

gaps.sentence: There ___ be a supervisor present when students use the lab.
Library books ___ be taken out of the reading room.
gaps.hint: a passive prohibition with mustn't be
gaps.explanation: Prohibitions can be passive: mustn't be taken.

gaps.sentence: He ___ have missed the train — he left home two hours early.
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have' expresses near-certainty that something did not happen: can't have missed.

gaps.sentence: Employees ___ use company computers for personal downloads.
gaps.hint: a formal prohibition with may not
gaps.explanation: Formal rules use 'may not' (or 'must not') for prohibitions: may not.

gaps.sentence: I have no idea where he is — he ___ have gone to the gym, or maybe to the pool.
gaps.hint: an uncertain guess about the past
gaps.explanation: 'Might have' expresses an uncertain guess about the past: might have gone.

gaps.sentence: You have been travelling all day, so you ___ be exhausted.
gaps.hint: an obvious conclusion from known facts
gaps.explanation: A logical conclusion from known facts uses 'must': must be exhausted.

gaps.sentence: You ___ better not be late again; the boss is getting tired of it.
gaps.explanation: The negative of 'had better' places 'not' after 'better': had better not be.
